clinicalPearls: DSM-5 (2022) replaced the older terms dependence and addiction with opioid use disorder, opioid intoxication, and opioid withdrawal; the disorder is defined as repeated use over a 12-month period causing problems in two or more domains (tolerance, withdrawal, using larger amounts than intended, craving, and continued use despite adverse consequences) (Harrison 22e p.3688).

The mu receptor is the receptor most clinically relevant to opioid effects; mu actions include analgesia, euphoric reinforcement, cough and appetite suppression, decreased respiration, decreased GI motility, sedation, and hormonal changes, while kappa activation tends to produce dysphoria and psychotic symptoms (Harrison 22e p.3689).

An opioid 'high' occurs only when the rate of rise in dopamine is fast, so rapid routes such as smoking and intravenous injection produce a 'rush' whereas oral and transdermal routes give analgesia/sedation without the euphoric high (Harrison 22e p.3689).

Opioid overdose is recognized clinically by shallow, slow respirations, pupillary miosis (mydriasis appears only after significant brain anoxia), bradycardia, hypothermia, and stupor or coma; immediate management is based on clinical criteria rather than waiting for toxicology (Harrison 22e p.3690).

Fentanyl overdose may require roughly twice the reversal-agent dose needed for other opioids, and reversal antagonists are short-acting relative to most opioids, so re-sedation can occur after an initial response (Harrison 22e pp.3688, 3690).

Adding xylazine (a nonopioid veterinary sedative) to illicit fentanyl markedly worsens respiratory suppression and is associated with tissue necrosis and increased risk of limb amputation in people who inject (Harrison 22e p.3690).
Opioids generally do not cause seizures except in unusual situations: polydrug use with meperidine, high-dose tramadol, or the newborn (Harrison 22e p.3690).

Withdrawal risk has a strong genetic component (up to ~50% related to functional polymorphisms), including a mu-opioid receptor variant conferring threefold higher affinity for opioids and beta-endorphin; epigenetic methylation may compensate by reducing mu-receptor numbers (Harrison 22e p.3689).

Methadone can prolong the QT interval (rates reported as high as ~16% above non-methadone injecting patients) and has caused sudden death; QT monitoring is relevant during overdose and maintenance (Harrison 22e pp.3690, 3691).

Heroin users are frequently polydrug users (alcohol, sedatives, cannabinoids, stimulants); none substitute for opioids but they have additive effects, so concurrent alcohol or sedative withdrawal (which can be more dangerous) must be excluded before managing opioid withdrawal (Harrison 22e p.3690).

Buprenorphine's partial agonism means escalating doses shift toward antagonist activity, so primary buprenorphine overdose is nearly impossible, but high doses can precipitate withdrawal in patients on full agonists such as morphine or methadone (Harrison 22e pp.3690-3691).
Most opioid-using individuals meet more than three diagnostic criteria, so reducing the DSM threshold from three to two problem areas did not change measured disease rates (Harrison 22e p.3688).
harrison.pathophysiology: Opioid receptors (mu, kappa, delta, nociceptin/orphanin) are G protein-linked and coupled to the cyclic AMP (cAMP) second-messenger system and to G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium channels (GIRKs); receptor binding increases potassium permeability, hyperpolarizes neurons, and inhibits action potentials, producing analgesia, sedation, and reinforcement. Reinforcing euphoria is mediated through the mesolimbic dopaminergic pathway from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens, where opioids indirectly raise dopamine by inhibiting GABAergic interneurons; the subjective high requires a fast rate of dopamine change. Tolerance and withdrawal arise from adaptive upregulation of the cAMP-PKA-CREB cascade in locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons after chronic mu-receptor inhibition: sustained inhibition triggers compensatory increases in cyclic AMP enzyme activity, so abrupt opioid cessation produces unopposed noradrenergic overactivity and withdrawal symptoms; this model underlies the use of alpha2-agonists to suppress that activation. PKA-driven phosphorylation of CREB also induces genes such as tyrosine hydroxylase and BDNF, the latter implicated in long-term neuroplastic changes (Harrison 22e pp.3689-3690).
additionalDifferentials: Concurrent sedative-hypnotic (benzodiazepine) overdose or withdrawal, which may coexist and be more dangerous to manage
Alcohol intoxication or withdrawal in a polydrug user
Other causes of coma with respiratory depression (CNS structural lesion, metabolic encephalopathy) before miosis-based diagnosis is confirmed
nonInfectiousMimics: Toxic megacolon from severe opioid-induced constipation mimicking primary abdominal catastrophe
MPTP-induced parkinsonism from contaminated illicitly synthesized meperidine, mimicking idiopathic Parkinson disease
Orthostatic hypotension from opioid-related histamine release mimicking other causes of hypotension
additionalInvestigations: Blood or urine toxicology to confirm a suspected opioid diagnosis (management must not wait for results)
ECG for QT-interval monitoring, particularly with methadone or in overdose
Arterial/clinical assessment of respiratory status and gag reflex (aspiration pneumonia risk in overdose)
Liver function tests when considering opioid-antagonist relapse-prevention therapy (most providers avoid it if LFTs exceed about three times normal)
Screening for blood-borne infection (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV) in people who inject
redFlags: Shallow/slow respirations with pinpoint miosis, bradycardia, hypothermia, and stupor or coma indicating life-threatening overdose
Mydriasis in a suspected overdose suggesting significant brain anoxia has supervened
Limited or absent response to standard reversal dosing, prompting suspicion of fentanyl, high antagonist requirement, or concurrent benzodiazepine overdose
Loss of gag reflex with aspiration pneumonia risk
Skin necrosis or limb compromise suggesting xylazine-adulterated fentanyl use
Septic complications of injection use such as meningitis, osteomyelitis, or organ abscesses
harrison.prognosis: Opioid use disorder is a chronic, relapsing condition; most patients tend to relapse during or after detoxification, and stopping use is far easier than preventing relapse. Long-term relapse prevention requires combined pharmacologic and psychosocial approaches. Medication-free inpatient/outpatient programs have poor 1- to 5-year outcomes compared with pharmacotherapy, except for residential programs lasting roughly 6-18 months. Untreated potentially lethal overdose progresses to respiratory and cardiovascular collapse and death. Globally the World Drug Report attributes the greatest burden of drug-related morbidity and mortality to opioid misuse; in 2022 over 76,000 US overdose deaths involved opioids, with rates accelerating due to high-potency fentanyl derivatives and stimulant co-use (Harrison 22e pp.3688, 3691-3692).
pitfalls: Administering so much antagonist that opioid withdrawal is precipitated, rather than targeting reversal of respiratory depression
Assuming a single antagonist dose is sufficient, since antagonists last only a few hours while most opioids persist longer, risking re-sedation (close monitoring/continuous antagonism often needed)
Overlooking concurrent benzodiazepine or alcohol/sedative involvement when reversal has only limited effect
Misjudging dose in naive or infrequent users because actual ingested potency is hard to estimate, especially with fentanyl derivatives
Forgetting that buprenorphine and methadone themselves can be misused and that buprenorphine can precipitate withdrawal in fentanyl- or high-dose-methadone-dependent patients
harrison.severityClassification: Withdrawal time course (heroin): symptoms begin ~8-10 h after the last dose, with early lacrimation, rhinorrhea, yawning, and sweating; later stages bring restless sleep, weakness, chills, piloerection ('cold turkey'), nausea/vomiting, muscle aches, involuntary movements, hyperpnea, hyperthermia, and hypertension. Acute withdrawal lasts ~7-10 days, followed by a protracted abstinence phase of ~26-30 weeks (hypotension, bradycardia, hypothermia, mydriasis, blunted respiratory CO2 responsiveness). Tolerance/withdrawal can develop within ~6-8 weeks of chronic daily use. Plasma half-lives vary widely: ~2.5-3 h for morphine, >22 h for methadone, minutes for fentanyl-related opioids, and longest for buprenorphine/metabolites (Harrison 22e pp.3689-3690).
